title: An atom and its electron cloud
alt: A live 3D view of the electron of a hydrogen atom in an s state: a cloud of dots where it is likely to be found, the surface where its wavefunction has one fixed size and, from n = 2 on, the spherical radial node shells where it is never found. Beside it, the curve of the probability of finding the electron at each distance from the nucleus, with the most probable distance marked.
sentences: An atom is a nucleus with electrons around it, but an electron is not a tiny ball on an orbit.
Quantum mechanics gives a cloud of probability instead: the 3D view shows that cloud around the nucleus, and the curve beside it shows how likely the electron is to be found at each distance.
Everything later in DFT is about these clouds, and about how they overlap and rearrange when atoms meet.

title: A wavefunction and an orbital
alt: A live 3D view of one hydrogen orbital as the surface where its wavefunction has one fixed size, orange where it is positive and blue where it is negative: a round s orbital, a p orbital with two lobes, or a d orbital (3d z2) with two lobes and a ring. Beside it, a slice through the same kind of orbital's cloud.
sentences: The wavefunction is the quantity that holds everything about one electron, and an orbital is the shape of one allowed wavefunction.
The s cloud is a ball, the p clouds have two lobes, and the d clouds are more complex still.
These shapes decide which neighbouring atoms an electron can bond with, which is why they matter for materials.

title: The exponential wall
alt: Curve of how many ways there are to place a growing number of electrons in their orbitals, on a powers-of-ten scale, where it looks almost straight because each added electron multiplies the count by about the same factor; labels give the count at the end and that factor.
sentences: To describe N electrons exactly, you have to keep track of every way of placing all of them at once, and the number of ways explodes as N grows.

The curve counts those ways when N electrons share 4N orbitals, and because each extra electron multiplies the count by roughly ten, the almost straight line on this powers-of-ten scale is really an explosion.
That wall is why DFT swaps the many-electron wavefunction for the electron density, which needs only one number per point in space however many electrons there are.
read: Left to right: more electrons.
Up: the number of ways (determinants) in powers of ten, so each notch up the axis means ten times more.
The labels give the count at the end of the curve and how much the last electron multiplied it.

title: Density as a map
alt: The electron density of electrons in a one-dimensional box, drawn twice: as a curve whose height is the charge at each place, and as a shaded strip below it with the same numbers as a map, darker where there is more charge and empty at the walls.
sentences: A many-electron wavefunction tracks every electron at once, but the electron density asks a simpler question: how much electron charge sits at each point?
Here electrons fill the levels of a one-dimensional box, two per level; the curve is the density and the strip below shows the same numbers as a map, darker where there is more charge.
Hohenberg and Kohn proved that this one map is enough, in principle, to fix the ground-state energy, and that is the idea DFT is built on.

try.label: Number of electrons in the box

read: Curve: its height is how much charge sits at that place in the box.
Strip: the same curve seen from above, like a heat map; in a real crystal the map fills three dimensions.
Add electrons: they fill higher levels, which have more bumps, so the map gains detail while the walls stay empty.

title: The Kohn-Sham idea
alt: A one-dimensional toy atom after a self-consistent run: the electron density as a filled curve and, optionally, the shared effective potential as a dashed well, each named on the picture.
sentences: Real electrons push on each other all the time, and that is what makes the exact many-electron problem so hard.
Kohn and Sham swapped them for stand-in electrons that ignore each other and instead all move in one shared potential, built so that together they have the same density as the real electrons.
The catch is a loop: the potential is built from the density, and the density comes from electrons moving in that potential, so the two have to agree.
read: Filled curve: the electron density of a one-dimensional toy atom, highest where the electrons are most likely to be.
Dashed curve: the shared potential every stand-in electron feels; the electrons gather in its low middle.
The next station shows the loop that makes the density and the potential agree.

title: The self-consistency loop
alt: A toy self-consistency loop, step by step: on top the density that goes into the chosen step in bold, earlier steps dotted and the converged answer dashed; below, one bar per step for how much the density changed, on a powers-of-ten scale, shrinking until it drops below the dashed stopping line.
sentences: The loop starts from a guess for the density, builds the potential from it, solves for the electrons in that potential and gets a new density.
The new density is mixed with the old one and goes in as the next guess, and this repeats until the density going in and the density coming out agree.
Move the slider through the steps of a toy run: the bold curve walks toward the dashed final answer, and the bars underneath shrink until the change is small enough to stop.
read: Top: the density going into the chosen step (bold), the earlier steps (dotted) and the final answer (dashed).
Bottom: one bar per step for how much the density changed; the scale counts powers of ten, so every equal step down is ten times smaller.
The dashed line is the stopping point; VASP stops the same way when the energy change falls below EDIFF.

title: The crystal and its unit cell
alt: A cube-based unit cell with its atoms drawn inside the cell edges.
sentences: A crystal is one small block of atoms, the unit cell, repeated in every direction.
The box in the picture is the cell; its lengths and angles and the positions of the atoms inside it are all that VASP needs to know about the structure.
Change the cell type to see how one idea gives different arrangements of atoms.

title: Periodic images
alt: Rock-salt unit cell shown once or repeated in all directions, so that the same block of atoms appears in every neighbouring cell.
sentences: VASP treats your cell as repeating forever, so an atom that leaves one side comes back in on the opposite side.
Repeating the cell in the picture shows this: every copy holds the same atoms in the same places.
That is why a small cell can stand in for a whole crystal, and why a molecule needs empty space around it so that its copies do not interact.

title: Plane waves and the ENCUT sphere
alt: A square grid of dots, each one plane wave of a square toy cell, with a circle whose radius is set by the cutoff energy: dots inside are filled and kept, dots outside are open and dropped, with the number kept. Beside it, a long wave for a dot near the centre and a short wave for a dot far out.
sentences: VASP builds each electron's wavefunction out of plane waves, simple waves that repeat neatly across the cell.
Each dot in the picture is one plane wave of a square toy cell: dots near the centre are long, gentle waves and dots far out are short waves with high kinetic energy.
ENCUT draws a circle (a sphere in 3D) and keeps only the waves inside it, so a higher cutoff keeps more waves, costs more time and gives more reliable energies, which is why you test it.
read: Filled dots: waves kept. Open dots: waves dropped.
The radius grows with the square root of ENCUT, so doubling ENCUT does not double the circle.
In a real 3D cell the count grows faster, roughly as ENCUT to the power 3/2.

title: Real space and reciprocal space
alt: Two panels side by side for a two-dimensional lattice. Left, real space: the atoms as dots, the cell vectors a1 and a2 and the shaded unit cell, lengths in angstrom. Right, reciprocal space: the reciprocal lattice as open dots, the vectors b1 and b2 and the shaded first Brillouin zone, lengths in 1/angstrom. A longer cell vector gives a shorter reciprocal vector.
sentences: Real space is the space you know: it says where the atoms are, and its cell vectors a1 and a2 are measured in angstroms.
Reciprocal space describes the waves that fit the crystal instead: its vectors b1 and b2 are measured in 1/angstrom, and each one is at right angles to the other cell vector.
The two work like a seesaw, so a longer cell vector gives a shorter reciprocal vector, and a big cell has a small Brillouin zone that needs fewer k-points.
read: Left: the atoms (dots), the cell vectors a1 and a2 and the unit cell, shaded.
Right: the reciprocal lattice (open dots), b1 and b2, and the Brillouin zone, shaded: the points closer to the centre than to any other dot.
Pick Rectangle: a2 doubles, b2 halves and the zone gets thinner in that direction.

title: Reciprocal space and the Brillouin zone
alt: The three real-space lattice vectors of a face-centred cubic cell and the three reciprocal vectors that go with them, drawn in one picture.
sentences: In three dimensions the same rule gives three reciprocal vectors, and their repeat unit is the Brillouin zone.
Each point in the zone is a k-point: one wave pattern that electrons in the crystal can have.
The picture shows the real-space cell vectors with the reciprocal vectors that match them; only directions and relative lengths are meaningful.

title: k-points: sampling the zone
alt: A live 3D view of a regular grid of k-points filling the cubic Brillouin zone of a simple cubic crystal, with the points that symmetry makes different marked larger; beside it, the same kind of grid laid over a square zone. The slider sets the number of points along each direction.
sentences: VASP cannot visit every k-point, so it samples the zone on a regular grid, the mesh you write in KPOINTS.
A finer mesh samples the zone better and costs more time, because each k-point is a separate calculation.
How fine is fine enough is found by testing, not by a fixed rule.

title: Bands and the density of states
alt: Two panels on one energy axis: on the left the two bands of a toy chain with two atoms per cell, energy against wave vector k, the lower band filled; on the right the density of states as horizontal bars, tall where the bands are flat. A dashed Fermi level crosses both, inside a gap for the insulator and where the bands touch for the metal.
sentences: In a crystal the electron energies are not single levels but bands: each wave vector k has its own energy, and together they sweep out a range.
The left panel draws those energies against k for a toy chain, and the right panel counts how many states sit at each energy; that count is the density of states, or DOS.
Electrons fill the states up to the Fermi level, so if it lies in a gap the material is an insulator, and if a band crosses it the material is a metal.
read: Shaded band: filled with electrons. Upper band: empty.
Where a band is flat, many k share nearly one energy, so the DOS bar there is long.
Pick Metal: the gap closes and the bands touch at the Fermi level.

title: Spin up and down, and magnetic orderings
alt: Eight atoms in a cube each carrying an arrow for the direction of its magnetic moment, arranged as ferromagnetic or as A, C or G type antiferromagnetic.
sentences: Electrons carry spin, so a magnetic atom acts like a tiny arrow, and VASP follows spin up and spin down separately when you set ISPIN = 2.
Neighbouring arrows can all point the same way (ferromagnetic) or alternate in the patterns called A, C and G antiferromagnetic.
The picture is a hand-set arrangement of arrows and not a result: which pattern has the lowest energy is for a calculation to say.

title: Your first VASP folder
alt: Flow diagram of the four input files in a VASP folder, POSCAR, INCAR, KPOINTS and POTCAR, going into the program that writes the output files.
sentences: A VASP run reads four input files from one folder: POSCAR, INCAR, KPOINTS and POTCAR.
POSCAR holds the structure, INCAR the settings, KPOINTS the sampling mesh and POTCAR the pseudopotentials.
The Input Builder writes the first three for you; POTCAR comes from your VASP licence and this site never hosts it.
